messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Inverse-lengthscale parameterized cov_exp_quad()?
parts:
Great to see the new cov_exp_quad() function in v2.12.0, but I see that it's been parameterized with a lengthscale argument, whereas I think a good argument could be made for inverse-lengthscale (see section on Gaussian Processes at bottom of https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations). 

Obviously users preferring inverse-lengthscale can transform before using cov_exp_quad() as is, but that's an extra operation. Indeed, where the formula in the cov_exp_quad() description involves 1/(2*lengthscale^2), parameterization with inverse-lengthscale should actually eliminate one operation. Admittedly, I don't know enough to assert whether there'd be a real-world performance difference between these cases, but thought it worth raising the point.

Thoughts?

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Re: Inverse-lengthscale parameterized cov_exp_quad()?
parts:
Ok, pretty embarrassed to have asserted that there's an extra computation with the lengthscale parameterization : P Obviously cov_exp_quad() doesn't compute 1/(2*lengthscale^2) then multiply by the squared euclidian distance term, but instead just divides the latter value by 2*lengthscale^2. 

Still, those of us that actively want to assert priors on inverse-lengthscale (though maybe just me?) will have to compute lengthscale=1/inverse_lengthscale before using cov_exp_quad() as is.

While I'm being compute stingy, is there any reason for the parameterization as dx/2l^2 rather than dx/z? The squaring then doubling of the lengthscale parameters aren't really necessary computationally, just in terms of interpretation after the fact. Or possibly I'm missing a nuanced reason for it being easier to imagine a prior for l rather than z (let alone 1/z)?

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Inverse-lengthscale parameterized cov_exp_quad()?
parts:
Hi Mike,

Keep asking questions! Hopefully you'll make use of this function. Our plan is to roll out more covariance kernels. I also don't speak for the whole development team -- I'm just answering them from my own perspective.

Regarding parameterization: we went with the Rasmusen and Williams parametrization from "Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning." I've seen a handful of implementations, including GPStuff, and other mathematical descriptions like wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_process) and the kernel cookbook (http://www.cs.toronto.edu/~duvenaud/cookbook/index.html) and they all parameterize it by length scale. It's a non-trivial amount of developer work to have multiple parameterizations. It also makes it more difficult on the user when they have choices to make regarding parameterization. There are a few cases where the demand has been high enough to warrant a second parameterization (I'm thinking negative binomial), but honestly, it's been more trouble than it's worth with user error, buggy code, and just giving users choice. For the version after v2.12.0, we'll have a faster version of the function for what we're thinking is a going to be a more common use of the function. Rob's gone and analytically computed the gradients for the function instead of using autodiff, but not for every use of the function. We've just introduced this function. I'm more interested in adding additional kernels rather than adding a reparameterization. In terms of work, they're on the same order of effort. Hopefully you feel the same. And... if you're into computation, we'll take help!

Regarding being compute stingy: this is a low order concern. When you're computing distances of two arrays of vectors, a divide isn't going to hurt. What's going to be useful is parameterizing the problem correctly. Rob's got some tricks up his sleeve that you might be interested in. I didn't look at the math, but it sounds like there's a modeling trick where a product is identifiable, but most people parameterize by the two factors. I think it's along those lines, but I could be wrong. Anyway, I know how the cov_exp_quad() function is built and a single divide isn't going to make a dent in the computation time.

Still, those of us that actively want to assert priors on inverse-lengthscale (though maybe just me?) will have to compute lengthscale=1/inverse_lengthscale before using cov_exp_quad() as is.
Yup. And that's easy!

While I'm being compute stingy, is there any reason for the parameterization as dx/2l^2 rather than dx/z? The squaring then doubling of the lengthscale parameters aren't really necessary computationally, just in terms of interpretation after the fact. On Wed, Sep 7, 2016 at 10:28 PM, Mike Lawrence <mike....@gmail.com> wrote:
Great to see the new cov_exp_quad() function in v2.12.0, but I see that it's been parameterized with a lengthscale argument, whereas I think a good argument could be made for inverse-lengthscale (see section on Gaussian Processes at bottom of https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations).  

Obviously users preferring inverse-lengthscale can transform before using cov_exp_quad() as is, but that's an extra operation. Indeed, where the formula in the cov_exp_quad() description involves 1/(2*lengthscale^2), parameterization with inverse-lengthscale should actually eliminate one operation. Admittedly, I don't know enough to assert whether there'd be a real-world performance difference between these cases, but thought it worth raising the point.

I think there's a bigger point to be made here. Speeding up the computation of a Stan program by a small percent isn't really that useful. You'll be a little faster, but you probably could have saved the effort and let the program run for just that much longer. The results will be identical, you'll have the same estimates for effective samples, etc. Where you're going to make big jumps are when you think about the parameterization of the Stan program in relation to the data you have. Although the Stan language is designed to be agnostic to the inference algorithms, when you start talking efficiency, you'll need to take into account the algorithm that's being run. If you're running with defaults, it's NUTS and you'll need to think about the joint lpdf of the data and the parameters on the unconstrained scale. But... if you're able to parameterize the problem correctly, you could get massive jumps in efficiency (orders of magnitude / correct vs incorrect). If you're looking to do thinks more efficiently, that's where I would turn; not shaving a handful of operations.

I think most of the devs would agree that shaving a few operations isn't how we'd go about making a Stan program go fast. Of course, I understand the desire to do that. It's easy (almost every program can be written just a little bit faster) and the alternative isn't always clear. In this case, I'd just forget about the cost of a divide.

Whenever the interface you're using catches up to 2.12, just for kicks, could you try using the length scale parameter in one program and in another try inverting twice -- so parameter l, transformed parameters inv_l = 1 / l and l2 = 1 / inv_l. Use inv_l in the cov_exp_quad() function. Set seeds and see if there's any noticeable time difference. (you could even put it in the model block if you want it to be run every leapfrog step.)

 

Thoughts?

That's it for now. Maybe someone else will chime in, but back to your original question -- I don't think we'll be adding a second parameterization soon. If you wanted to do it, we'd welcome it.



Daniel

Mike
